summary: Contrasts the "document" point of view, where digital objects are like pieces of paper read by people, with the "protocol" point of view, where objects are dynamic network messages. It argues that sticking to the document view can damage protocol design and that understanding both helps avoid conflicts.

plainLanguage.summary: A letter is made to be read by a person, but a message between computers is more like a plug that must fit exactly. Designing one as if it were the other causes trouble.

questions: document versus protocol point of view
why protocol design differs from document design
subtitle: Why protocol design and document design require different approaches.

tldr.problem: Standards work increasingly involves higher-level application constructs and syntaxes beyond low-level binary protocols. Participants with a document-oriented mindset (thinking of digital objects like pieces of paper) conflict with those with a protocol mindset (thinking of network messages), causing design problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC contrasts two points of view through detailed examples: the document view emphasizes human-readable meaning, direct presentation, and minimal modification; the protocol view emphasizes computer processing, complex composition, and necessary transformation. Understanding both clarifies design decisions in security, canonicalization, and extensibility.
tldr.outcome: Protocols designed with a document point of view tend to be inefficient, overly complex, and insecure. Better designs start with the protocol point of view and add document elements only as necessary for consensus.

today: RFC 3930 is an Informational RFC that remains relevant to anyone involved in protocol and standards design. It documents a recurring tension in IETF standards work that continues to affect how protocols and formats are specified.

sections.title: Two Different Design Perspectives
sections.content:
Much of the IETF's traditional work has focused on low-level binary protocol constructs, viewed from the protocol point of view: digital objects are composite dynamic network messages created by a source process and consumed by a destination process. But as higher-level application constructs and syntaxes are involved in standards work, people with a document point of view become involved, thinking of digital objects as pieces of paper written and viewed by people.

These two viewpoints are fundamentally different. Those accustomed to one viewpoint frequently struggle to understand the other. Even when they grasp it intellectually, they tend to assume their preferred viewpoint applies broadly and slip back into using it by default. This clash is not merely academic; adherence to a document point of view can damage protocol design. By understanding both, conflicts between them can be clarified and reduced.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people think about network messages like computer scientists: they are puzzles that must fit together exactly. Others think like writers: they are documents that people read and should look nice. They do not understand each other.

sections.title: Core Differences in Meaning and Processing
sections.content:
The document view treats digital objects as analogous to pieces of paper. A major concern is presenting such documents to a third party (such as a court) as directly as possible. Anything affecting what a person sees—including style sheets—is considered part of the document. This perspective sometimes forgets that documents originate, travel, and are processed in computer systems.

The protocol view treats digital objects as bits on the wire generated and consumed by computer processes. No person sees the full message; it is only viewed as translated text when debugging. If something must be demonstrated in court, computer experts must interpret it. This perspective sometimes forgets that pieces of messages may end up being displayed to people.

These views also differ on processing. Documents are thought of as quasi-static objects that are transferred whole or combined with minimal modification. Protocols expect complex processing where different message pieces are handled differently, some forwarded to other processes, with rich multilevel structures and components that may be processed separately from their context.
sections.plainLanguage: Document people think: keep the whole thing together and unchanged. Protocol people think: take it apart, process each piece separately, put it back together. Both happen on computers, but they do not think the same way.

sections.title: Security, Canonicalization, and Authentication
sections.content:
Canonicalization is the transformation of information into a standard form, discarding insignificant details (such as changing line endings to a standard encoding). The document view treats canonicalization as suspect or outright evil: if someone modifies a piece of paper to standardize its format, that is an unauthorized change. Digital signatures should work like signatures on paper—they do not justify any standardization of the document. The protocol view, by contrast, treats canonicalization as a necessity: you must define what parts of the bits are significant, process them consistently, and handle insignificant variations.

In practice, any complex protocol system that uses digital signatures must choose between three bad options: too little canonicalization (brittle signatures that fail on insignificant changes), too much canonicalization (insecure signatures that pass when important data changes), or the difficult middle ground of selecting appropriate canonicalizations. Only the third option works. Thus, signed protocol messages require canonicalization as part of signing and verification, a truth that later protocol extensions and revisions will reinforce repeatedly.

For authentication, the document view prefers digital signatures (asymmetric key) and rejects message authentication codes because the verifier could forge them. The protocol view treats these as engineering decisions affecting efficiency and security model. Practical protocol messages comprise various pieces with different sources, destinations, and security requirements; a signature covering the whole message makes little sense, and some fields (like hop counts) are rarely worth signing.
sections.plainLanguage: Document people say: "Do not change anything, and sign the whole paper." Protocol people say: "Change what does not matter, sign the pieces that do." The document way breaks easily; the protocol way is hard to design but it works.

sections.title: Extensibility and Versioning
sections.content:
When protocols will need future extensions, the design question is how to handle versions and new features gracefully. The document view does not usually consider extensibility a major problem. The assumption is that a design with a simple version scheme will meet all requirements, or that knowledge of new versions can be easily distributed to all sites. This approach works in closed systems with central control, such as SGML/DTD systems.

The protocol view assumes protocols will always need extension and that not all implementations can be updated synchronously. This is a difficult problem, but protocol designers try to provide tools: carefully defined versioning and feature labeling, negotiation of versions where possible, clear specifications of how different versions interact, length-delimited data so unknown elements can be skipped, and destination labeling so intermediaries know whether to process or pass through data.

These approaches lead to very different structures. Document-oriented designs often become unwieldy and brittle when extended. Protocol designs that anticipate evolution can grow gracefully across many years and interoperability boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Document people assume: "We will design it right once and not change much." Protocol people assume: "Things will change forever, so plan for it now." Real systems prove protocol designers right.

sections.title: Reconciling the Views
sections.content:
The protocol point of view can nearly encompass the document view as a limiting case when: message complexity declines to a single payload with few attachments, the payload mutability declines to a standard format needing little canonicalization, the number of parties and processing steps decline, and the message portion intended for human consumption increases. Under these constraints, protocol perspective narrows to something close to the document view. Even when the document view is questionable, adding options to a protocol (non-canonicalization options, optional policy statements, semantic labels) often mollifies those thinking from that view.

The document point of view, however, is difficult to stretch to encompass typical protocol cases. Strict document thinking—canonicalization is wrong, every significant object needs human-language policy text, every adjunct needs semantic tags—produces objects rarely suitable for protocol use: improperly structured for hierarchy and complexity, inefficient due to unnecessary text, and insecure due to brittle signatures.

Therefore, the best approach is to start with the protocol point of view and add document point of view elements only as necessary to achieve consensus. This ensures that the underlying structure is sound, extensible, and secure, with accommodations for document-oriented needs added thoughtfully rather than driving the design.
sections.plainLanguage: Build it as a protocol first, because protocols can become simple documents but documents rarely become good protocols. Add document stuff only if people really need it.
